title: The digestive tract: a tube within a tube
summary: One continuous canal from mouth to anus, the accessory organs that pour into it, and the body plan around it.
objectives: List the organs of the alimentary canal in order
Name the accessory digestive organs and how they reach the canal
Explain the 'tube within a tube' body plan
takeaways: Alimentary canal: mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum, anus.
Accessory organs (teeth, tongue, salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, pancreas) never carry food through themselves; glands pour secretions in through ducts.
Body wall = outer tube; gut = inner tube; the body (peritoneal) cavity lies between.

steps.title: One long canal
steps.text:
The alimentary canal (gastrointestinal or GI tract) is one continuous tube: the oral cavity, pharynx, oesophagus (esophagus), stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum and anus.

Food moves through it by muscular contraction, is broken down by enzymes and acid, and the useful products are absorbed across its lining; what remains leaves as faeces.

check.q: Name the alimentary canal in order.
check.a: Oral cavity, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum, anus.

steps.title: The accessory organs
steps.text:
The accessory digestive organs help without food passing through them. Teeth and the tongue work in the mouth. The salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas are glands or reservoirs that deliver saliva, bile and pancreatic juice through ducts.

The liver and pancreas are large enough to be organs in their own right, and both also do non-digestive jobs.

check.q: Does food pass through the pancreas?
check.a: No: it is an accessory organ that sends its juice into the duodenum through a duct.

steps.title: A tube within a tube
steps.text:
The body is built as a tube within a tube. The body wall is the outer tube; the digestive tract is the inner one. Between them lies the body cavity (in the abdomen, the peritoneal cavity), lined by serous membrane.

The space inside the gut, its lumen, is open to the outside at both ends. Strictly, food in the lumen is not yet inside the body until it is absorbed.

check.q: In the tube-within-a-tube plan, what forms the outer tube and what the inner?
check.a: Outer: the body wall. Inner: the digestive tract, with the body cavity between them.

practice.q: Put the alimentary canal in order
Which is an accessory digestive organ?
practice.why: Accessory organs secrete into the canal but carry no food.

practice.q: List the accessory digestive organs.
practice.a: Teeth, tongue, salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, pancreas.

title: Mouth, palate and the muscles of chewing
summary: The walls of the mouth, a tongue that is almost all muscle, and the four muscles that close the jaw.
objectives: Describe the boundaries and lining of the oral cavity
Describe the tongue, its frenulum and its roles in eating
Group the muscles that close, open and grind the jaw
takeaways: Roof: hard palate (maxillae + palatine bones) in front, soft palate and uvula behind.
Lined by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.
Tongue: skeletal muscle; genioglossus is the main extrinsic muscle.
Masseter and temporalis close; pterygoids grind; digastric and platysma help open.

steps.title: Walls of the mouth
steps.text:
The oral cavity opens between the lips (labia); a labial frenulum ties each lip to the gingiva (gums). The roof is the hard palate — palatine processes of the maxillae plus the palatine bones — continued behind by the muscular soft palate with its hanging uvula, which blocks the nasal cavity during swallowing.

The floor of the mouth lies below the tongue, and at the back the fauces open into the oropharynx. A non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium resists abrasion.

check.q: Which bones form the hard palate?
check.a: The palatine processes of the maxillae and the palatine bones.

steps.title: The tongue
steps.text:
The tongue is a mass of skeletal muscle covered by mucosa. Its largest extrinsic muscle, the genioglossus, fans back from the mandible and protrudes the tongue. The lingual frenulum anchors its underside to the floor of the mouth.

It shapes speech, carries taste buds, pushes food between the teeth, and in swallowing forms a bolus and pistons it back into the oropharynx.

check.q: Name four jobs of the tongue.
check.a: Speech, taste, moving food to the teeth, and forming and pushing the bolus into the oropharynx.

steps.title: Muscles of mastication
steps.text:
Two powerful muscles of mastication close the jaw: the masseter on the side of the face and the temporalis fanning over the temple. The medial and lateral pterygoids, deep to the ramus, slide the mandible side to side so premolars and molars grind.

Opening is helped by gravity and by muscles below the jaw: the digastric and the thin platysma of the neck depress the mandible.

check.q: Which two muscles elevate the mandible most powerfully?
check.a: Masseter and temporalis.

practice.q: Which muscles grind food side to side?
practice.why: Masseter and temporalis close; digastric and platysma open.

practice.q: What anchors the lips to the gums, and the tongue to the floor of the mouth?
practice.a: The labial frenulum and the lingual frenulum.

practice.q: What epithelium lines the oral cavity, and why?
practice.a: Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, which resists abrasion.

practice.q: What is the fauces?
practice.a: The opening at the back of the mouth into the oropharynx.

title: Tongue papillae and taste buds
summary: Four kinds of papillae, only three of which taste, and the cell that turns a molecule into a signal.
objectives: Name and describe the four types of lingual papillae
Describe the cells of a taste bud and how a taste cell signals
Relate the posterior tongue to the tonsils and epiglottis
takeaways: Filiform: most numerous, keratinised, no taste buds, friction.
Fungiform (mushroom), foliate (leaf-like, lateral) and vallate (large, V-shaped row) carry taste buds.
Taste bud: gustatory cells with taste hairs at a taste pore, supporting cells and basal cells.
Taste cells synapse onto sensory nerve fibres.

steps.title: Four kinds of papillae
steps.text:
The dorsal surface of the tongue is roughened by papillae that add friction. Filiform papillae are thread-like, the most numerous, keratinised and carry no taste buds. Fungiform papillae are mushroom-shaped and scattered among them.

Foliate papillae are leaf-like folds on the sides at the back. The large vallate (circumvallate) papillae, each ringed by a trench, stand in a V-shaped row in front of the sulcus terminalis.

check.q: Which papillae have no taste buds?
check.a: The filiform papillae.

steps.title: Inside a taste bud
steps.text:
Taste buds sit mainly on the sides of vallate and foliate papillae and the tops of fungiform ones. Each is a barrel of cells: gustatory (taste) cells, supporting cells, and basal cells that replace them.

Each taste cell sends a taste hair (microvilli) up to the taste pore on the surface. At its base it synapses onto the terminal of a sensory neuron, releasing neurotransmitter from synaptic vesicles.

check.q: What projects through the taste pore?
check.a: The taste hairs (microvilli) of the gustatory cells.

steps.title: The back of the tongue
steps.text:
Behind the vallate papillae the tongue curves down into the oropharynx. The palatine tonsils sit in the side walls there, and the epiglottis stands just behind the root of the tongue.

In a cat, the dorsum is covered with stiff, backward-pointing keratinised filiform papillae — the rasp used for grooming.

check.q: What makes a cat's tongue rough?
check.a: Keratinised, backward-pointing filiform papillae on its dorsal surface.

practice.q: Which papillae form a V-shaped row at the back of the tongue?
practice.why: Vallate (circumvallate) papillae are the largest.

practice.q: Which cells replace worn-out taste cells?
practice.why: Basal cells are the stem cells.

practice.q: Name the three cell types in a taste bud.
practice.a: Gustatory (taste) cells, supporting cells, basal cells.

practice.q: How does a taste cell signal to the brain?
practice.a: It synapses onto a sensory neuron terminal, releasing transmitter from synaptic vesicles.

practice.q: Where are foliate papillae?
practice.a: Leaf-like folds on the lateral sides of the posterior tongue.

title: Teeth: structure, types and dental formulas
summary: Enamel, dentin, pulp and cementum; four shapes of tooth; twenty milk teeth and thirty-two permanent.
objectives: Name the regions and tissues of a tooth
Describe how a tooth is anchored in its socket
Identify incisors, canines, premolars and molars and their jobs
Write the deciduous and permanent dental formulas
takeaways: Crown (enamel) above the gum, neck at the gum line, root (cementum) in the socket.
Pulp cavity → root canal → apical foramen carries nerves and vessels.
Periodontal ligament holds the tooth in the alveolar socket: a gomphosis.
Per quadrant: deciduous I2 C1 M2 (20 teeth); permanent I2 C1 P2 M3 (32 teeth).

steps.title: Crown, neck and root
steps.text:
Every tooth has a crown exposed above the gum, a neck at the gum line, and one or more roots buried in the jaw. The biting surface of back teeth rises into cusps.

Teeth sit in alveolar sockets of the maxilla and mandible, in an upper (maxillary) and a lower (mandibular) arch.

check.q: Which part of the tooth lies at the gum line?
check.a: The neck.

steps.title: The tissues of a tooth
steps.text:
Enamel, the hardest substance in the body, caps the crown. Beneath it the bulk of the tooth is bone-like dentin. The root is covered by cementum.

In the centre, the pulp cavity holds nerves and blood vessels; it continues through each root as the root canal, which they enter at the apical foramen. Periodontal ligaments tie the cementum to the socket wall — a fibrous joint called a gomphosis.

check.q: Through what opening do nerves and vessels enter the tooth?
check.a: The apical foramen.

steps.title: Four shapes for four jobs
steps.text:
Incisors are flat, chisel-like blades that nip and cut. Canines (cuspids) have one pointed cusp for tearing. Premolars (bicuspids) have two cusps and grind. Molars have three to five cusps and do the heaviest grinding.

An adult has 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars and 12 molars, including four third molars (wisdom teeth).

check.q: How many cusps does a bicuspid have, and what is its other name?
check.a: Two; a premolar.

steps.title: Two sets of teeth
steps.text:
Children have 20 deciduous (primary, milk) teeth: no premolars, and only 8 molars. The dental formula gives the teeth in one quadrant: deciduous I2 C1 P0 M2; permanent (secondary) I2 C1 P2 M3, which × 4 quadrants = 32.

Milk teeth erupt from about 6 months (lower central incisors, 6–8 months) to about 2 years (second molars, 20–24 months), and are shed between roughly 6 and 12 years.

check.q: Write the permanent dental formula for one quadrant.
check.a: I2 C1 P2 M3 (8 teeth; 32 in all).

practice.q: How many deciduous teeth are there?
practice.why: No premolars, 8 molars.

practice.q: Which is the hardest substance in the body?
practice.why: Enamel caps the crown.

practice.q: Put the tissues in order from the surface of the crown inward
Give the deciduous dental formula for one quadrant.
practice.a: I2 C1 P0 M2 (20 teeth in total).

practice.q: What holds a tooth in its alveolar socket?
practice.a: Periodontal ligaments (a gomphosis joint) attaching cementum to the socket wall.

practice.q: What are wisdom teeth?
practice.a: The third molars.

practice.q: When do the first and last deciduous teeth usually erupt?
practice.a: Central incisors at 6–8 months; second molars at 20–24 months.

title: The salivary glands
summary: Three pairs of glands, a litre or so of saliva a day, and where each duct opens.
objectives: Name the three paired salivary glands and locate them
Trace each duct to its opening
State what saliva contains and does
Identify the cat salivary glands and the veins crossing them
takeaways: Saliva (1–1.5 L/day): water, mucus and salivary amylase.
Parotid duct crosses masseter, pierces buccinator, opens opposite the upper second molar.
Submandibular duct opens under the tongue beside the lingual frenulum.
Sublingual gland: floor of mouth, many small ducts.

steps.title: Three pairs of glands
steps.text:
Three pairs of glands make most of our saliva, about 1–1.5 L a day: the parotid, submandibular and sublingual glands.

Saliva is mostly water. Its mucus lubricates and binds food into a bolus, and salivary amylase starts the digestion of starch.

check.q: Which enzyme in saliva begins starch digestion?
check.a: Salivary amylase.

steps.title: The parotid gland
steps.text: The parotid gland is the largest, lying in front of the ear over the masseter. Its parotid duct runs forward across the masseter, turns in and pierces the buccinator in the cheek (buccal region), and opens inside the mouth opposite the upper second molar.

check.q: Where does the parotid duct open?
check.a: Inside the cheek opposite the upper second molar.

steps.title: Submandibular and sublingual
steps.text:
The submandibular gland lies medial to the body of the mandible. Its submandibular duct runs forward to open under the tongue, beside the lingual frenulum.

The sublingual gland is the smallest, lying in the floor of the mouth under the tongue, and empties through many small ducts.

check.q: Which salivary gland drains through many small ducts?
check.a: The sublingual gland.

steps.title: Salivary glands in the cat
steps.text:
In the cat the cream-coloured parotid sits below and in front of the ear, with its duct crossing the masseter. The submandibular gland lies near the angle of the mandible, beside the digastric, with the smaller sublingual gland just in front of it.

Two veins cross them: the cat's posterior facial vein (our retromandibular vein) and anterior facial vein (our facial vein).

check.q: What is the human equivalent of the cat's posterior facial vein?
check.a: The retromandibular vein.

practice.q: Which gland is the largest?
practice.why: It lies in front of the ear.

practice.q: Trace the parotid duct
items: Opening opposite the upper second molar

practice.q: What does saliva contain?
practice.a: Water, mucus (lubricant) and salivary amylase.

practice.q: Where does the submandibular duct open?
practice.a: Under the tongue beside the lingual frenulum.

practice.q: Which veins cross the cat salivary glands, and their human names?
practice.a: Posterior facial vein (retromandibular vein) and anterior facial vein (facial vein).

title: Pharynx, swallowing and the oesophagus
summary: Three constrictors, three kinds of muscle down the oesophagus, and a sphincter that keeps acid down.
objectives: Divide the pharynx and say what passes through each part
Describe how the pharyngeal constrictors and peristalsis move a bolus
Describe the course, muscle and wall of the oesophagus
Explain the lower oesophageal sphincter and reflux
takeaways: Nasopharynx: air. Oropharynx: food and air. Laryngopharynx: to larynx and oesophagus.
Oesophagus: C6 to stomach through the oesophageal hiatus; skeletal above, smooth below.
Stratified squamous lining and an adventitia, not a serosa.
A failing lower oesophageal sphincter lets acid reflux: heartburn, GERD.

steps.title: The pharynx
steps.text: The nasopharynx runs from the internal nares (choanae) to the soft palate and carries air only. The oropharynx, from the soft palate to the epiglottis, carries food, liquid and air, so it is lined by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium. The laryngopharynx, behind the larynx, leads into both the larynx and the oesophagus.

check.q: Why is the oropharynx lined by stratified squamous epithelium?
check.a: It carries food as well as air, so it needs an abrasion-resistant lining.

steps.title: Swallowing
steps.text:
The tongue pushes the bolus back into the oropharynx. The soft palate rises to close the nasopharynx and the epiglottis folds over the larynx. Then the superior, middle and inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscles contract in sequence, squeezing the bolus down into the oesophagus.

From there, waves of peristalsis — a ring of contraction behind the bolus, relaxation ahead of it — carry it to the stomach.

check.q: What is peristalsis?
check.a: A wave of muscular contraction behind the bolus, with relaxation ahead, that pushes it along.

steps.title: The oesophagus
steps.text:
The oesophagus begins at about C6, runs down behind the trachea, passes through the oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm and joins the stomach. Its muscle is skeletal in the upper third, mixed in the middle and smooth in the lower third.

It is lined by stratified squamous epithelium, and its outer coat is an adventitia of loose connective tissue, not a serosa. The space inside is the lumen.

check.q: What kind of muscle is in the lower third of the oesophagus?
check.a: Smooth muscle.

steps.title: The lower oesophageal sphincter
steps.text:
Where the oesophagus meets the cardia of the stomach, a thickened ring of smooth muscle acts as the lower oesophageal (cardiac or gastro-oesophageal) sphincter. It relaxes to let a bolus in and otherwise stays closed so acid cannot flow back.

When it fails, acid reflux burns the squamous lining: heartburn, and when chronic, GERD (gastro-oesophageal reflux disease).

check.q: What does the lower oesophageal sphincter prevent?
check.a: Reflux of stomach acid into the oesophagus.

practice.q: At which vertebral level does the oesophagus begin?
practice.why: It continues from the laryngopharynx at the lower border of the cricoid.

practice.q: The outer coat of the thoracic oesophagus is:
practice.why: It lies in the mediastinum, not in a serous cavity.

practice.q: Put the muscle types down the oesophagus in order
What is GERD, and what fails to cause it?
practice.a: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (heartburn): the lower oesophageal sphincter fails to hold back stomach acid.

practice.q: Where does the nasopharynx begin and end?
practice.a: From the internal nares (choanae) to the soft palate.

title: The gut wall and the peritoneum
summary: Four layers that never change, two nerve plexuses, and the serous sheets that hang the gut in place.
objectives: Name the four layers of the GI wall and the parts of the mucosa
Place the submucosal and myenteric plexuses and say what each controls
Distinguish visceral and parietal peritoneum, mesentery and omenta
Name retroperitoneal organs
takeaways: Mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae), submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa/adventitia.
Submucosal (Meissner) plexus: secretion. Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus: motility.
Visceral peritoneum = serosa on organs; parietal peritoneum lines the wall; mesentery joins them.
Kidneys, pancreas and most of the duodenum are retroperitoneal.

steps.title: Four layers
steps.text:
From the lumen outward the wall has four tunics. The mucosa (mucous membrane) is epithelium, a lamina propria of loose connective tissue, and a thin muscularis mucosae. The submucosa is connective tissue carrying blood vessels, lymphatics and, in places, glands with ducts.

The muscularis externa is inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle that mixes and propels. Outermost is the serosa — thin connective tissue plus a simple squamous mesothelium — or an adventitia.

check.q: Name the three parts of the mucosa.
check.a: Epithelium, lamina propria and muscularis mucosae.

steps.title: The gut's own nervous system
steps.text:
The enteric nervous system is two nerve networks in the wall. The submucosal (Meissner) plexus in the submucosa controls secretion and local blood flow; the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus, between the circular and longitudinal muscle, drives motility.

The mucosa also holds lymphatic nodules (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) and tube-shaped intestinal glands (crypts).

check.q: Which plexus lies between the two muscle layers, and what does it control?
check.a: The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus; gut motility.

steps.title: Peritoneum and mesentery
steps.text:
The parietal peritoneum lines the body wall; the visceral peritoneum is the serosa on the organs. Between them is the peritoneal cavity with a film of fluid.

A mesentery is a double fold of peritoneum joining the gut to the posterior body wall and carrying its blood vessels, lymphatic vessels and nerves. The embryonic dorsal mesentery hangs the gut from behind; the ventral mesentery becomes the lesser omentum and the liver's ligaments.

check.q: What does a mesentery carry?
check.a: Blood vessels, lymphatic vessels and nerves to and from the gut.

steps.title: Behind the peritoneum
steps.text:
Retroperitoneal organs lie behind the parietal peritoneum, against the posterior body wall. The kidneys are the classic example; so are the pancreas, most of the duodenum, and the ascending and descending colon.

In a cross-section they sit beside the lumbar vertebra and erector spinae, with the lower ribs above them, while the peritoneal organs hang forward on mesenteries.

check.q: What does retroperitoneal mean?
check.a: Lying behind the parietal peritoneum, against the posterior body wall, without a mesentery.

practice.q: Put the layers of the gut wall in order from the lumen
The serosa is the same as the:
practice.why: Connective tissue plus simple squamous mesothelium.

practice.q: Which is retroperitoneal?
practice.why: It lies behind the parietal peritoneum.

practice.q: What makes up the enteric nervous system?
practice.a: The submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses.

practice.q: What is the difference between the dorsal and ventral mesentery?
practice.a: The dorsal mesentery hangs the gut from the posterior wall; the ventral mesentery (in the upper abdomen only) becomes the lesser omentum and the liver's ligaments.

practice.q: What are lymphatic nodules in the gut mucosa?
practice.a: Clusters of lymphocytes (MALT) guarding the lining.

title: The stomach
summary: A muscular acid bath: its regions, its extra layer of muscle, and the cells of its glands.
objectives: Name the regions and curvatures of the stomach
Describe the three-layered muscularis and the gastric mucosa
Name the gastric gland cells and their products
takeaways: Cardia, fundus, body, pylorus (antrum + canal); pyloric sphincter at the exit.
Three muscle layers: inner oblique, middle circular, outer longitudinal.
Gastric pits lead to gastric glands; no villi.
Parietal cells: HCl. Chief cells: pepsinogen, activated by acid to pepsin.

steps.title: A reservoir and mixer
steps.text:
The stomach sits in the left upper quadrant. It stores a meal and churns it with hydrochloric acid (HCl) and enzymes into a soupy chyme.

Its contents can reach pH 1–2. Acid this strong denatures proteins, opening them up for enzymes, and kills most swallowed microbes.

check.q: What is chyme?
check.a: The semi-liquid mix of food, acid and enzymes the stomach produces.

steps.title: Regions and curvatures
steps.text:
The cardia surrounds the oesophageal opening. The fundus domes above it; the body is the main part; the pylorus — the pyloric antrum and narrow pyloric canal — ends at the pyloric orifice, guarded by the pyloric sphincter that meters chyme into the duodenum.

The convex left border is the greater curvature, the concave right one the lesser curvature. Inside, folds called rugae flatten as the stomach fills.

check.q: What are rugae for?
check.a: They are mucosal folds that let the stomach distend as it fills.

steps.title: A wall built to churn
steps.text:
Uniquely, the stomach's muscularis has three layers: an inner oblique, a middle circular and an outer longitudinal. The extra oblique layer lets it wring and churn.

The mucosa is simple columnar epithelium dimpled by gastric pits, each leading down into tubular gastric glands. There are no villi and few goblet cells: instead every surface cell secretes mucus.

check.q: Name the three muscle layers of the stomach from inside out.
check.a: Inner oblique, middle circular, outer longitudinal.

steps.title: The gland cells
steps.text:
Surface mucous cells coat the lining with protective alkaline mucus, and mucous neck cells sit in the gland necks. Parietal cells (pink or orange on a slide) secrete HCl and intrinsic factor. Chief cells (blue, basophilic) at the gland base secrete pepsinogen.

Acid converts pepsinogen into pepsin, a proteolytic enzyme that starts protein digestion. Enteroendocrine cells release hormones such as gastrin into the blood.

check.q: Which cells secrete HCl and which pepsinogen?
check.a: Parietal cells: HCl. Chief cells: pepsinogen.

practice.q: Put the stomach regions in order from oesophagus to duodenum
Pepsinogen is converted to pepsin by:
practice.why: Parietal-cell acid activates the chief-cell zymogen.

practice.q: Which feature identifies stomach mucosa?
practice.why: Villi belong to the small intestine.

practice.q: What does the pyloric sphincter do?
practice.a: Controls the outflow of chyme from the stomach into the duodenum.

practice.q: What do enteroendocrine cells secrete?
practice.a: Hormones such as gastrin, into the blood.

practice.q: What lies at the bottom of a gastric pit?
practice.a: One or more tubular gastric glands.

title: The small intestine
summary: Five metres of absorbing surface in three parts you can tell apart under the microscope.
objectives: Give the length and parts of the small intestine and what each receives
Describe a villus and where its absorbed products go
Tell duodenum, jejunum and ileum apart histologically
takeaways: Duodenum ~25 cm, jejunum ~2 m, ileum ~3 m; ~5 m in life.
Villus core: capillaries (sugars, amino acids → portal vein) and a lacteal (fats → lymph).
Duodenum: Brunner glands. Jejunum: tall villi, neither marker. Ileum: Peyer patches.
The ileocecal valve stops backflow from the large intestine.

steps.title: Three parts, five metres
steps.text:
The small intestine is the main site of nutrient absorption: about 5 m long in life (longer in a relaxed cadaver) and 3–4 cm wide.

The duodenum (~25 cm) is a C-shaped, mostly retroperitoneal loop that receives bile and pancreatic juice. At the duodenojejunal flexure it becomes the jejunum (~2 m), then the ileum (~3 m), which ends at the ileocecal valve. The mesentery suspends jejunum and ileum.

check.q: Which part of the small intestine receives bile and pancreatic juice?
check.a: The duodenum.

steps.title: Villi
steps.text:
Villi are finger-like mucosal projections that multiply the surface area; they are the hallmark of small intestine. They are covered by simple columnar absorptive cells with a brush border, and scattered goblet cells that secrete mucus.

In each core, capillaries take up sugars and amino acids, which travel to the liver in the hepatic portal vein. A central lacteal takes up fats into the lymph. Lymphocytes patrol the lamina propria.

check.q: Where do absorbed fats go, and where do sugars go?
check.a: Fats into the lacteal (lymph); sugars and amino acids into the capillaries → hepatic portal vein.

steps.title: Duodenum versus jejunum
steps.text:
The duodenum is identified by duodenal (Brunner) glands in the submucosa. They secrete alkaline mucus that protects the lining from the acid chyme arriving from the stomach.

The jejunum has the tallest, most numerous villi and tall circular folds, but neither Brunner glands nor Peyer patches.

check.q: What do Brunner glands secrete, and why?
check.a: Alkaline mucus, to protect the duodenal lining from acid chyme.

steps.title: The ileum
steps.text:
The ileum carries Peyer patches — aggregated lymphoid nodules in the mucosa and submucosa, often on the side opposite the mesentery. They sample gut contents and start immune responses.

The ileum ends at the ileocecal junction, where the ileocecal valve stops backflow from the large intestine.

check.q: Which histological feature identifies the ileum?
check.a: Peyer patches (aggregated lymphoid nodules).

practice.q: Put the small intestine in order
Brunner glands in the submucosa identify the:
practice.why: They neutralise acid chyme.

practice.q: Which segment is longest?
practice.why: The duodenum is the shortest.

practice.q: What is a lacteal?
practice.a: The lymphatic capillary in the core of a villus, which absorbs fats.

practice.q: What does the ileocecal valve do?
practice.a: Prevents backflow from the large intestine into the ileum.

practice.q: How does a jejunum slide differ from an ileum slide?
practice.a: Jejunum: tall villi, no Peyer patches. Ileum: Peyer patches (aggregated lymphoid nodules).

title: The large intestine
summary: From cecum to anus: taeniae and haustra, the appendix, water absorption and the blood supply.
objectives: Name the parts of the large intestine in order
Describe the cecum, appendix, taeniae coli, haustra and omental appendages
Describe the rectum and anal canal, defecation and haemorrhoids
State the arterial supply and the histology of the colon
takeaways: Cecum → ascending colon → right colic flexure → transverse → left colic flexure → descending → sigmoid → rectum → anal canal → anus.
Three taeniae coli pucker the wall into haustra; fat tags are omental appendages.
SMA: cecum to mid-transverse colon. IMA: distal colon and rectum.
Colon mucosa: straight crypts packed with goblet cells, no villi, no Peyer patches.

steps.title: The frame around the abdomen
steps.text:
The large intestine is about 1.4 m long and 7 cm wide. It absorbs water and forms faeces (feces).

In order: cecum → ascending colon → right colic (hepatic) flexure → transverse colon → left colic (splenic) flexure → descending colon → sigmoid colon → rectum → anal canal → anus. The transverse and sigmoid colons hang on mesenteries, the transverse and sigmoid mesocolons.

check.q: Which flexure lies next to the spleen?
check.a: The left colic (splenic) flexure.

steps.title: Cecum and appendix
steps.text:
The cecum is a blind pouch below the ileocecal valve. Attached to it near the valve is the finger-sized vermiform appendix, whose wall is rich in lymphoid tissue.

If its narrow lumen is blocked it can become inflamed: appendicitis.

check.q: Where is the vermiform appendix attached?
check.a: To the cecum, near the ileocecal valve.

steps.title: Taeniae, haustra and fat tags
steps.text:
The longitudinal muscle of the colon is gathered into three bands, the taeniae coli (teniae coli). Their tone puckers the wall into pouches called haustra.

Small fat-filled tags of peritoneum, the omental (epiploic) appendages, hang from the surface. Together these three features identify colon at a glance.

check.q: What produces the haustra?
check.a: The tone of the three taeniae coli gathering the wall into pouches.

steps.title: Rectum, anal canal and defecation
steps.text:
The S-shaped sigmoid colon lies in the left iliac (inguinal) region. It joins the straight rectum in the pelvis, which becomes the short anal canal opening at the anus.

Faeces are stored in the sigmoid colon and rectum until mass peristalsis fills the rectum and triggers defecation. Enlarged rectal and anal (haemorrhoidal) veins are haemorrhoids (hemorrhoids).

check.q: What are haemorrhoids?
check.a: Enlarged (varicose) rectal/anal veins.

steps.title: Blood supply and histology
steps.text:
The superior mesenteric artery supplies the cecum to about two-thirds along the transverse colon; the inferior mesenteric artery supplies the rest of the colon and the rectum. Both leave the abdominal aorta.

Colon mucosa is simple columnar epithelium with very many goblet cells in straight crypts. It has no villi (unlike small intestine) and solitary lymphatic nodules but no Peyer patches.

check.q: How does colon mucosa differ from small intestine and stomach?
check.a: No villi (unlike small intestine) and many goblet cells (unlike stomach).

practice.q: Put the large intestine in order
Which artery supplies the cecum?
practice.why: SMA: cecum to mid-transverse colon.

practice.q: What triggers defecation?
practice.a: Mass peristalsis moving faeces into the rectum, stretching it.

practice.q: Name three surface features that identify colon.
practice.a: Taeniae coli, haustra and omental (epiploic) appendages.

title: The liver
summary: The biggest gland: its lobes and ligaments, the porta hepatis, and the lobule where blood meets bile.
objectives: List the main functions of the liver
Name the four lobes and the falciform, round and coronary ligaments
Describe what enters and leaves at the porta hepatis
Describe the liver lobule, portal triad, sinusoids, Kupffer cells and bile flow
takeaways: Right, left, quadrate (by gallbladder) and caudate (by IVC) lobes.
Falciform ligament with the round ligament (old umbilical vein) in its free edge; coronary ligament around the bare area.
Porta hepatis: portal vein and hepatic artery in, hepatic ducts out.
Lobule: central vein, hepatocyte plates, sinusoids, portal triads; bile flows opposite to blood.

steps.title: The body's chemical works
steps.text: The liver is the largest gland, in the right upper quadrant under the diaphragm. It processes the nutrient-rich blood arriving from the gut, stores nutrients such as glycogen, makes plasma proteins, carries out detoxification of drugs and toxins, and produces bile.

check.q: Name four functions of the liver.
check.a: Processing absorbed nutrients, storing glycogen, making plasma proteins, detoxification, producing bile.

steps.title: Lobes and ligaments
steps.text:
The large right lobe and smaller left lobe are divided on the front by the falciform ligament, which attaches the liver to the diaphragm and anterior wall. In its free edge runs the round ligament (ligamentum teres), the remnant of the umbilical vein.

On the underside, the quadrate lobe lies beside the gallbladder and the caudate lobe behind, next to the IVC. The coronary ligament surrounds the bare area, which has no peritoneum.

check.q: What is the round ligament of the liver a remnant of?
check.a: The fetal umbilical vein.

steps.title: The porta hepatis
steps.text:
The porta hepatis is the liver's doorway on its visceral surface. The hepatic portal vein (nutrient-rich, deoxygenated blood from the gut) and the hepatic artery proper (oxygenated blood) enter; the hepatic ducts carrying bile leave.

Blood leaves by a different route: hepatic veins drain into the inferior vena cava, which runs in a groove on the back of the liver.

check.q: Which vessels enter the liver at the porta hepatis?
check.a: The hepatic portal vein and the hepatic artery proper.

steps.title: The liver lobule
steps.text:
Microscopically the liver is built of roughly hexagonal liver lobules. A central vein sits in the middle, with hepatic cords (plates of hepatocytes) radiating from it. At the corners are portal triads: a branch of the hepatic artery, a branch of the hepatic portal vein and a bile duct.

Arterial and portal blood mix in the sinusoids between the plates and flow toward the central vein, then to the hepatic veins.

check.q: Name the three vessels of a portal triad.
check.a: A hepatic artery branch, a hepatic portal vein branch and a bile duct.

steps.title: Kupffer cells and bile
steps.text:
The sinusoids are lined by leaky endothelium and by Kupffer cells: stellate macrophages that remove bacteria and old red cells from portal blood.

Hepatocytes secrete bile into tiny bile canaliculi between neighbouring cells. Bile flows outward toward the bile ducts of the triads — the opposite direction to the blood, which flows inward to the central vein.

check.q: Which way does bile flow in a lobule, relative to blood?
check.a: Outward toward the portal triads, opposite to the blood flowing in to the central vein.

practice.q: Trace portal blood through the liver
Which ligament separates the right and left lobes anteriorly?
practice.why: The round ligament runs in its free edge.

practice.q: What surrounds the bare area of the liver?
practice.a: The coronary ligament.

practice.q: What are hepatic cords?
practice.a: Plates of hepatocytes radiating from the central vein.

title: Bile ducts, gallbladder and pancreas
summary: Where bile goes between meals and after them, and a gland that is both exocrine and endocrine.
objectives: Explain how bile emulsifies fat
Trace bile from the liver to the gallbladder and on to the duodenum
Describe the hepatopancreatic ampulla and the duodenal papillae
Describe the parts, neighbours and two secretions of the pancreas
takeaways: Hepatic ducts → common hepatic duct → cystic duct → gallbladder (storage).
Gallbladder → cystic duct → common bile duct → ampulla → major duodenal papilla.
Accessory pancreatic duct → minor duodenal papilla.
Pancreas: acini make enzymes and bicarbonate; islets make insulin and glucagon.

steps.title: What bile does
steps.text:
Bile is made continuously by the liver and stored and concentrated in the gallbladder, which lies in a fossa on the underside of the liver.

Its bile salts act like detergent: they break fat globules into tiny droplets (emulsification). Lipids are not digested by bile itself, but the extra surface area lets pancreatic lipase work far faster.

check.q: Does bile digest fat?
check.a: No: bile salts emulsify it into small droplets so lipase has more surface to act on.

steps.title: Filling and emptying the gallbladder
steps.text:
The right and left hepatic ducts join as the common hepatic duct. Between meals the sphincter at the duodenum is closed, so bile backs up the cystic duct into the gallbladder.

When fatty chyme enters the duodenum the gallbladder contracts: bile runs down the cystic duct into the common bile duct and on to the duodenum.

check.q: Which duct carries bile both into and out of the gallbladder?
check.a: The cystic duct.

steps.title: The ampulla and the papillae
steps.text:
The common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct unite in the wall of the duodenum as the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater). It opens on the major duodenal papilla, guarded by the hepatopancreatic sphincter.

A smaller accessory pancreatic duct opens a little higher on the minor duodenal papilla.

check.q: Which two ducts join to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla?
check.a: The common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct.

steps.title: The pancreas in place
steps.text:
The pancreas is retroperitoneal, behind and below the stomach. Its head sits in the C of the duodenum, the body crosses the spine, and the tail reaches toward the spleen.

Along its upper border run branches of the coeliac trunk: the left gastric, common hepatic and, following the tail, the splenic artery.

check.q: Which part of the pancreas lies in the curve of the duodenum?
check.a: The head.

steps.title: Exocrine and endocrine
steps.text:
As an exocrine gland, the pancreas's acinar cells secrete digestive enzymes and its duct cells add bicarbonate, a buffer that neutralises acid chyme; both flow through the pancreatic duct to the duodenum.

As an endocrine gland, scattered pancreatic islets release insulin (beta cells) and glucagon (alpha cells) into the blood.

check.q: Which pancreatic secretion neutralises acid chyme?
check.a: Bicarbonate, from the duct cells.

practice.q: Trace bile from the liver to the gallbladder
Trace bile from the gallbladder to the duodenum
Pancreatic islets secrete:
practice.why: The endocrine pancreas.

practice.q: What is emulsification?
practice.a: Breaking large fat globules into small droplets (by bile salts).

practice.q: Where does the accessory pancreatic duct open?
practice.a: On the minor duodenal papilla.

title: The cat digestive system
summary: The same plan in a carnivore: a rasping tongue, a many-lobed liver, a tiny cecum and anal sacs.
objectives: Map the cat's mouth and pharynx structures to human equivalents
Describe the cat liver, stomach, omenta, spleen and pancreas
Describe the cat intestines and the features with no human match
takeaways: Cat tongue: keratinised filiform papillae; larynx close behind the tongue.
Cat liver has five lobes (right and left median, right and left lateral, caudate) and a green gallbladder.
J-shaped stomach on the left; long coiled small intestine; short large intestine.
No vermiform appendix; anal sacs beside the anus have no human equivalent.

steps.title: Mouth and throat
steps.text:
The cat's oral vestibule is the space between lips and cheeks and the teeth; the oral cavity proper lies inside the teeth, roofed by the hard palate and soft palate. The tongue, tied down by a lingual frenulum, is supported by the hyoid, mylohyoid and geniohyoid.

Behind, the nasopharynx (with the auditory tube openings), oropharynx with palatine tonsils, and laryngopharynx lead to the epiglottis and larynx — which sit closer to the tongue than ours — and to the oesophagus dorsal to the trachea.

check.q: What is the oral vestibule?
check.a: The space between the lips/cheeks and the teeth.

steps.title: Liver, stomach and spleen
steps.text:
The cat liver is divided into several lobes — right median, right lateral, left median, left lateral and caudate — with a green gallbladder and common bile duct. The stomach is J-shaped on the left, with rugae inside and a pyloric sphincter at the duodenum.

The greater omentum hangs from the greater curvature like a lacy apron; the lesser omentum joins stomach to liver. The spleen lies along the greater curvature, with the pancreas tail reaching it.

check.q: Name the lobes of the cat liver.
check.a: Right median, right lateral, left median, left lateral and caudate.

steps.title: Intestines and body cavity
steps.text:
A carnivore's gut is short overall: the cat's small intestine is long and coiled (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) and looks velvety from its villi, while the large intestine is short. Its cecum is a tiny pouch with no vermiform appendix, followed by ascending, transverse and descending colon and the rectum.

Beside the anus the cat has anal glands (anal sacs), with no human equivalent. Parietal and visceral peritoneum and the mesentery are as in us.

check.q: Which human digestive structure does the cat lack?
check.a: The vermiform appendix.

practice.q: How does the cat cecum differ from ours?
practice.why: The cat cecum is a small pouch without an appendix.

practice.q: Which cat structure has no human equivalent?
practice.why: They open beside the anus.

practice.q: Compared with a human, the cat larynx lies:
practice.why: The cat's larynx sits just behind the tongue.

practice.q: Describe the cat stomach.
practice.a: J-shaped, on the left; cardia, fundus, body, curvatures and pylorus, rugae inside, pyloric sphincter at the duodenum.

practice.q: What colour is the cat gallbladder, and which duct drains it to the duodenum?
practice.a: Green; via the cystic duct and the common bile duct.

practice.q: Which gut segments are long and short in the cat?
practice.a: Small intestine long and coiled (villi make it velvety); large intestine short.

practice.q: Name the three pharynx regions seen in the cat and what opens into the first.
practice.a: Nasopharynx (auditory tube openings), oropharynx, laryngopharynx.

practice.q: In the cat, where does the rectum lead and what surrounds the body cavity?
practice.a: The rectum leads to the anus; the body cavity is lined by parietal peritoneum, with visceral peritoneum on the organs.

title: The kidney: position, coverings and internal anatomy
summary: Two retroperitoneal beans behind the gut, their three wrappings, and the funnel system inside.
objectives: Name the organs of the urinary system and locate the kidneys
List the kidney's coverings from inside out
Describe what passes through the hilum and the renal vessels' origins
Identify cortex, medulla, pyramids, columns, papillae, calyces, pelvis and sinus
Compare the sheep and cat kidney
takeaways: Kidneys: retroperitoneal, T12–L3, right a little lower; adrenals on top.
Renal capsule → perirenal fat → renal fascia.
Hilum: renal artery in; renal vein and ureter out. Left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta.
Papilla → minor calyx → major calyx → renal pelvis → ureter.

steps.title: The urinary system
steps.text:
The urinary system is the two kidneys, two ureters, the urinary bladder and the urethra.

The kidneys lie retroperitoneal on the posterior abdominal wall at about T12–L3, partly sheltered by the lower ribs, in front of psoas major. The right sits slightly lower because the liver is above it. An adrenal (suprarenal) gland caps each superior pole.

check.q: Why is the right kidney slightly lower than the left?
check.a: The liver lies above it.

steps.title: Three wrappings
steps.text:
From the inside out: a tough renal (fibrous) capsule clings to the kidney surface; a cushion of perirenal fat (the adipose capsule, or renal fat pad) surrounds it; and the renal fascia anchors kidney and fat to the posterior wall.

In front lies the parietal peritoneum, which is why the kidney is retroperitoneal.

check.q: List the kidney's coverings from the inside out.
check.a: Renal (fibrous) capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia.

steps.title: The hilum and the renal vessels
steps.text:
The medial concave border has a slit, the hilum, where the renal artery enters and the renal vein and ureter leave. The renal arteries branch from the abdominal aorta; the renal veins drain into the inferior vena cava.

Because the IVC lies to the right, the left renal vein is longer and crosses in front of the aorta. Lower down the aorta and IVC divide into the common iliac arteries and veins.

check.q: Which renal vein is longer, and why?
check.a: The left, because it must cross in front of the aorta to reach the IVC on the right.

steps.title: Inside the kidney
steps.text:
A coronal (frontal) cut shows an outer renal cortex and an inner renal medulla. The medulla is a row of cone-shaped renal pyramids, separated by renal columns — inward extensions of cortex.

Each pyramid's tip, the renal papilla, drips urine into a minor calyx. Minor calyces join into major calyces, which form the renal pelvis, continuous with the ureter. The pelvis sits in the renal sinus with vessels and fat, like a hand in a glove.

check.q: What separates neighbouring renal pyramids?
check.a: Renal columns (extensions of cortex).

steps.title: Sheep and cat kidneys
steps.text:
A sheep kidney is the same bean shape. Its capsule peels off; at the hilum you find the renal artery, renal vein and ureter; and a coronal cut shows cortex, medulla, pyramids, papillae, calyces, pelvis and sinus.

In the cat the kidneys lie retroperitoneal against the dorsal wall in a renal adipose pad. The renal veins are larger than the arteries and drain into the posterior vena cava (our IVC) to the right of the spine, with the aorta on its left. The ureters run back to the bladder.

check.q: What is the human name for the cat's posterior vena cava?
check.a: The inferior vena cava.

practice.q: Trace urine from pyramid to ureter
At what vertebral levels do the kidneys lie?
practice.why: Partly protected by the lower ribs.

practice.q: What passes through the renal hilum?
practice.a: Renal artery (in), renal vein and ureter (out).

practice.q: In the cat, which is larger, renal artery or renal vein?
practice.a: The renal vein.

title: Renal blood flow and the nephron
summary: Blood through two capillary beds in a row, filtrate through a tubule, and how each looks on a slide.
objectives: Trace blood through the kidney from renal artery to renal vein
Describe the renal corpuscle and the parts of the renal tubule in order
Explain filtration, reabsorption and secretion
Tell PCT, DCT, collecting duct and loop apart on a slide
takeaways: Renal a. → segmental → interlobar → arcuate → cortical radiate → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries/vasa recta → veins back.
Nephron: glomerulus + glomerular capsule, then PCT → loop → DCT → collecting duct.
Filtration at the glomerulus; reabsorption mostly into the peritubular capillaries.
PCT: cuboidal with a fuzzy brush border. DCT: no brush border, clearer lumen.

steps.title: Blood in, blood out
steps.text:
The renal artery gives segmental arteries, then interlobar arteries running up the renal columns, arcuate arteries arching along the corticomedullary junction, and cortical radiate (interlobular) arteries climbing into the cortex. Each feeds afferent arterioles.

After the capillaries, blood returns by cortical radiate veins, arcuate veins, interlobar veins and the renal vein. The arcuate vessels mark the boundary between cortex and medulla.

check.q: Which vessels run along the boundary between cortex and medulla?
check.a: The arcuate arteries and veins.

steps.title: Two capillary beds in a row
steps.text:
The afferent arteriole feeds the glomerulus, a tuft of capillaries where plasma is filtered. Blood leaves by the efferent arteriole into a second bed: the peritubular capillaries around the tubules, the main site of reabsorption. Two capillary beds in series like this is a portal-type arrangement, sometimes called a renal portal system.

Juxtamedullary nephrons (~15%) have long loops, and their efferent arterioles form straight vasa recta that help concentrate urine; cortical nephrons (~85%) have short loops.

check.q: Which capillary bed filters, and which reabsorbs?
check.a: The glomerulus filters; the peritubular capillaries reabsorb.

steps.title: The nephron, in order
steps.text:
A nephron is a renal corpuscle plus a renal tubule. The corpuscle is the glomerulus inside the cup-shaped glomerular (Bowman) capsule; filtrate collects in the capsular space between its layers.

The tubule runs: proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) → nephron loop (loop of Henle: descending then ascending limb) → distal convoluted tubule (DCT), which returns to touch its own corpuscle → collecting duct, shared by many nephrons and running down the pyramid to a papilla.

check.q: Put the tubule segments in order.
check.a: PCT, nephron loop (descending then ascending limb), DCT, collecting duct.

steps.title: Making urine
steps.text:
Blood pressure drives filtration through the fenestrated glomerular capillaries. The filtrate is plasma without cells or large proteins. Along the tubule, reabsorption returns water, glucose and most electrolytes to the blood, and secretion adds unwanted substances. Urea becomes steadily more concentrated.

Where the DCT touches its afferent arteriole lies the juxtaglomerular apparatus, which regulates the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and releases renin. Constricting the afferent arteriole lowers GFR.

check.q: What happens to GFR if the afferent arteriole constricts?
check.a: It falls: less blood and pressure reach the glomerulus.

steps.title: Reading a kidney slide
steps.text:
In the cortex, round glomeruli sit among cross-cut tubules. The capsule's parietal layer is simple squamous epithelium; its visceral layer is podocytes wrapping the capillaries. The PCT is simple cuboidal with a brush border of microvilli that makes its lumen look fuzzy, and pink cytoplasm. The DCT has no brush border, a clearer lumen and paler cells.

In the medulla, parallel collecting ducts have cuboidal cells with crisp borders, and thin loop segments are simple squamous.

check.q: How do you tell a PCT from a DCT on a slide?
check.a: The PCT has a brush border (fuzzy lumen) and pinker cytoplasm; the DCT has none and a clearer lumen.

practice.q: Trace blood through the kidney
Trace filtrate through the nephron
About what proportion of nephrons are juxtamedullary?
practice.why: Cortical nephrons are the other 85%.

practice.q: What epithelium forms the PCT, and what marks it?
practice.a: Simple cuboidal epithelium with a brush border of microvilli.

practice.q: What is the renal corpuscle?
practice.a: The glomerulus plus the glomerular (Bowman) capsule.

practice.q: What are the vasa recta?
practice.a: Straight capillaries from juxtamedullary efferent arterioles running beside the long loops in the medulla; they help concentrate urine.

title: Ureters, bladder and urethra
summary: Peristalsis down the ureters, a stretchy bladder with a smooth trigone, two sphincters and two urethras.
objectives: Describe the ureter wall and how urine moves
Describe the bladder, detrusor, rugae and trigone
Describe transitional epithelium empty and stretched
Explain the sphincters and the micturition reflex
Compare the female and male urethra
takeaways: Ureter: transitional epithelium, smooth muscle, adventitia; peristalsis.
Trigone: between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice.
Internal sphincter: smooth, involuntary. External sphincter: skeletal, voluntary.
Female urethra 3–4 cm; male ~20 cm: prostatic → membranous → spongy.

steps.title: The ureters
steps.text:
Each ureter is a long, thin, retroperitoneal tube from the renal pelvis to the bladder. Its wall is a mucosa of transitional epithelium on a lamina propria, a layer of smooth muscle, and an outer adventitia.

Urine is pushed along by peristalsis, not gravity. The ureters enter the back of the bladder obliquely at the ureteric orifices, so a full bladder squeezes them shut.

check.q: How does urine move down the ureter?
check.a: By peristalsis of its smooth muscle.

steps.title: The bladder
steps.text:
The urinary bladder lies just behind the pubic symphysis, below and in front of the parietal peritoneum (anteperitoneal). Its wall is smooth muscle, the detrusor muscle, which contracts to empty it; when empty, the mucosa folds into rugae.

On the posterior wall is a smooth triangle, the trigone, between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice. It is a common site for infection.

check.q: What are the three corners of the trigone?
check.a: The two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice.

steps.title: Transitional epithelium
steps.text:
The bladder is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), a stratified epithelium on a basement membrane over the lamina propria. In the relaxed, empty bladder its surface (umbrella) cells are dome- or teardrop-shaped; they do not flatten as stratified squamous cells would.

As the bladder fills, stretch (distension) thins the layer and the surface cells flatten, letting it hold much more urine.

check.q: What happens to transitional epithelium when the bladder fills?
check.a: It thins and the dome-shaped surface cells flatten.

steps.title: Sphincters and micturition
steps.text:
At the bladder neck the internal urethral sphincter is involuntary smooth muscle. Lower down, in the urogenital diaphragm, the external urethral sphincter is voluntary skeletal muscle.

In the micturition reflex, stretch receptors in the filling bladder wall signal the spinal cord; the reflex contracts the detrusor and opens the internal sphincter. Urine flows only when we also relax the external sphincter voluntarily.

check.q: Which urethral sphincter is under voluntary control?
check.a: The external urethral sphincter (skeletal muscle).

steps.title: Two urethras
steps.text:
The female urethra is only 3–4 cm long; its external urethral orifice lies in front of the vaginal opening and behind the clitoris. Its shortness is why urinary bladder infections (UTIs) are commoner in women.

The male urethra (~20 cm) has three parts: prostatic (through the prostate gland), membranous (through the urogenital diaphragm, beside the bulbourethral glands) and spongy (penile, in the corpus spongiosum from the bulb of the penis to the glans). The crura of the penis anchor the erectile tissue of the corpora cavernosa.

check.q: Why are UTIs more common in females?
check.a: The female urethra is short (3–4 cm), so bacteria reach the bladder more easily.

practice.q: Put the male urethra in order from the bladder
The internal urethral sphincter is:
practice.why: The external sphincter is the voluntary one.

practice.q: Transitional epithelium in an empty bladder has surface cells that are:
practice.why: They flatten only when stretched.

practice.q: Describe the micturition reflex.
practice.a: Stretch receptors in the bladder wall → spinal reflex → detrusor contracts and internal sphincter opens; the external sphincter is relaxed voluntarily.

practice.q: In the female, where is the external urethral orifice?
practice.a: Anterior to the vaginal opening and posterior to the clitoris.

practice.q: Name the three layers of the ureter wall.
practice.a: Mucosa (transitional epithelium + lamina propria), smooth muscle, adventitia.

practice.q: What are the crus and bulb of the penis?
practice.a: The crura are the anchored proximal ends of the corpora cavernosa; the bulb is the expanded proximal end of the corpus spongiosum.
